doc.title: Derek Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 29, 1995

title: Whether jazz is oral culture; learning from records and players
summary: He answers that talent matters over education, and he learned from records then from playing with others.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: If it’s not her key they don’t know where to come in. Let me ask you this question. How do you feel that jazz is a representation of oral culture?
As compared to literate culture. I mean some of it’s on the page, but by all means not all of it’s not on the page.
I don’t know what you’re asking me. I can’t translate that into terms I can understand.
Oral culture is just information or education passed on sonically where you learn by sound, rather than by learning by literate culture through the page.

Well, if you’re really asking me whether jazz is a triumph of education over talent, no there’s no question about it. I think that the finest players are the guys who feel it here, and it comes out, and I’ll take a guy who really cannot play the instrument too well, but I recognize the signs of music coming out there, and it’s just a question before he can really do it better. I mean it would be embarrassing, I could name you names of people I’ve heard at early stages of development, and people say, “ah, the guy can’t play.” And I say, “listen, can’t you hear what he’s trying to play? He’s hearing it in his head, he just doesn’t know enough about the instrument yet to play it properly. Come back in a year or so.” I can think of certain guys who are wonderful now. And I don’t know whether that really answers your question.
Well you learned mostly from records.

Right, sure. I started learning from records. Then I think I learned mostly from playing with other guys. People do things when you’re playing. And it changes all your ideas. And that’s what I love about jazz, and you know I’m developing a solo act now simply because that’s the way it is, but I love that playing with all the guys, because just, whatever they feel about a song, or whatever you’re playing, it makes you play differently with their input. Because you all play off of each other.
